question: Why the travelling twin comes home younger

scene.title: Why the travelling twin comes home younger
scene.subtitle: Two twins part and meet again. A clock made of light shows why the one who travels counts fewer years.
scene.takeaway: A bent path through space and time holds less time. Only the traveller turns around, so only they come home younger.

beats.title: A map of space and time
beats.body: Up is time, sideways is distance from Earth. The dotted line is light, the fastest anything goes. Staying home, a twin’s path runs straight up, one dot per year.

beats.title: Why a moving clock ticks slowly
beats.body: A light clock ticks each time light crosses between two mirrors. Light moves at the same speed for everyone, as experiments since 1887 show. Seen from Earth, the mirrors move, so the light must slant to hit them: a longer path, so slower ticks.

beats.title: The trip
beats.body: Now the traveller flies to a star and back at 87% of light speed. The star is 3.5 light-years away (light takes 3.5 years), so each way takes 4 Earth years. Every clock on board slows the same way, and so does the traveller’s body. They meet after 8 years at home, but only 4 on the rocket.

beats.title: Why not the other way round?
beats.body: From the rocket, Earth seems to move, so shouldn’t Earth’s clock be the slow one? While both glide at steady speed, each twin does see the other’s clock run slow. But only the traveller turns around, pressed into their seat, so only their path bends. Between two meetings, the straight path holds the most time, though on this map the bent one looks longer.

scene.why: It is the clearest case of time being personal: clocks that take different paths really do show different times, as atomic clocks flown around the world in 1971 confirmed.
scene.opening: Two twins say goodbye. One stays home and one flies to a star and back. Why is the traveller younger when they meet again?

questions.q: If the traveller flew faster, would the age gap grow or shrink?
questions.a: Grow. A faster trip bends the path more, and a more bent path holds less time.

questions.q: From the rocket, the Earth is the one moving away. Why isn’t the home twin the younger one?
questions.a: Only the traveller’s path is bent: they turn around, and everyone agrees on that. The straight path between the two meetings holds the most time.

questions.q: What would a clock riding on a beam of light show?
questions.a: No time at all: light’s path has zero length in spacetime.
